messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Clinical Vignette: Dr. Aroha T.

Aroha was fifty-eight when a delivery truck ran a red light and struck her sedan broadside at an intersection in Portland. She remembered the sound—a terrible, metal-on-metal shriek—and then nothing coherent. The hospital records documented a fractured clavicle, a concussion, and lacerations, but what remained with her was not a narrative arc. It was fragments: the windshield exploding into her peripheral vision, the sickening tilt of the car, someone screaming—she could not later say if it was her. When she tried to reconstruct the sequence for the police report, the moments refused to order themselves. What came first, the impact or the spinning? Had she braced herself, or had she been thrown forward? Even now, months later, she could not tell a clear story of what happened, even to herself. The memory did not live in her mind as a sequence but as shards of sensation that erupted without warning—a flash of chrome, the smell of hot rubber, the pressure of the seat belt—appearing fully formed and visceral whenever some detail in her surroundings triggered them. A car alarm in the parking lot at the hospital where she worked sent her entire body into a state of recognition, as though the accident were happening again in real time.

Aroha had spent thirty years as a psychiatrist, trained to understand the architecture of trauma, yet she found herself unable to apply that knowledge to her own mind. The accident had revealed something she had come to believe was immutable: she was permanently changed for the worse. The woman who had driven to that intersection—competent, measured, someone others relied upon—no longer existed. In her place was someone who could not trust her own judgment. She had been hit by a truck she never saw coming; what else might she miss? What other dangers was she failing to perceive? The world revealed itself as fundamentally dangerous, and her own capacity to navigate it safely had been shattered. This conviction—that she was damaged in ways that could not be repaired—seemed to generate a cascading certainty: every unexpected noise, every car that moved too quickly through an intersection, became evidence of threat. The more she believed herself broken and the world hostile, the more she scanned for danger. Her eyes tracked vehicles with an intensity that exhausted her. She avoided driving on main roads, then on highways, then on anything but the quietest residential streets. Eventually she stopped driving altogether.

The fragmented quality of her memory seemed to feed this cycle. Because she could not construct a coherent narrative of the accident, she could not contain it. It lived in her body as raw sensation, triggered without warning by the most mundane stimuli—a car backfiring, the sight of a delivery truck, even certain angles of light through a windshield—and each time it was triggered, the memory felt fresh and uncontrollable, reinforcing her sense that the world was unsafe and she was powerless within it. Her inability to order what had happened meant she could not reassure herself that the accident was over, that she had survived, that she was safe now. The memory's formlessness kept the threat alive.

By autumn, Aroha had developed rigid rituals to manage the terror that seemed to live just beneath her skin. She could not go to sleep without checking every lock twice, and she could not lie in the dark—the darkness itself became a threat, a space where she could not see what was coming. She would lie awake for hours, her heart racing, waiting for dawn. When exhaustion finally claimed her, she would jolt awake in the small hours, her body drenched in sweat, and she would rise to walk through her house, checking that her back was never exposed to an open doorway. At work, she repositioned her chair so that she sat with her back against the wall, able to see the entire office. Her colleagues noticed but said nothing. She tried to suppress the fear, to control it through sheer force of will—she was a psychiatrist, after all, and she understood the pathology—but the effort of emotional containment only seemed to exhaust her further, leaving her more vulnerable to the intrusive thoughts that came unbidden: images of impact, of metal folding, of her own fragility. The more she tried not to think about the accident, the more insistent those thoughts became. The more she tried to control her fear, the more it leaked out in other ways—she could not bear to be touched, could not imagine intimacy, and had withdrawn from her ex-husband's attempts at friendship. Sex had become unthinkable, a vulnerability she could not permit herself.

What brought Aroha to seek treatment was not the fear itself—she had learned to live with that—but the recognition that the woman she had been was disappearing into the structures she had built to survive. She could no longer see her patients with the presence they deserved. She was failing at the very work that had defined her. She sat in the intake session with her back to the wall, her hands folded tightly in her lap, and said quietly: "I need to know if I can come back from this. I need to know if I'm still a doctor."
